action-reaction.title: Action and reaction
action-reaction.subject: Physics · Newton’s Third Law
action-reaction.problem: A 1500 kg car collides with a 200 kg motorbike. Which one exerts a greater force on the other at the moment of impact? And why?
action-reaction.feedback: Both exert the same force on each other. The motorbike moves more because of its smaller mass, not because the force is greater.
action-reaction.review: Both the car and the motorbike exert the same force on each other. Their accelerations differ because their masses differ.

force-pairs.title: Finding force pairs
force-pairs.subject: Physics · Newton’s Third Law
force-pairs.problem: When a student pushes a wall, identify the two objects and describe the force each object exerts. Why do the forces not cancel?
force-pairs.feedback: The student pushes the wall and the wall pushes the student with an equal and opposite force. They do not cancel because they act on different objects.
force-pairs.review: Every interaction includes two equal and opposite forces acting on two different objects.

balanced-forces.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
balanced-forces.subject: Physics · Forces and motion
balanced-forces.problem: A book is resting on a table. Describe the forces on the book and explain whether they are balanced. What would need to change for the book to move upward?
balanced-forces.feedback: The upward support force and downward gravitational force are balanced while the book rests. An upward net force would be needed for it to accelerate upward.
balanced-forces.review: Balanced forces give a zero net force; motion changes only when forces are unbalanced.

objective.title: Today’s objective
objective.text: Understand and apply Newton’s Third Law: when one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.

keyPoints.title: Key points
keyPoints.one: Forces always come in pairs: action and reaction.
keyPoints.two: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
keyPoints.three: They act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other.
keyPoints.four: Both forces happen at the same time.

questions.title: Teacher Q&A
questions.description: Official answers to common questions from today’s class.

cancel.question: Why don’t the two forces cancel each other out?
cancel.answer: They do not cancel because each force acts on a different object. Forces can only cancel when they act on the same object.

effect.question: Do action–reaction forces always have the same effect?
effect.answer: The forces are equal, but their effects can differ because the objects may have different masses and therefore different accelerations.

rest.question: Can one of the objects be at rest?
rest.answer: Yes. A wall may stay still when you push it, but it still exerts an equal and opposite force on you.
